strengths: Carefully designed 1D synthetic testbed enables rigorous mechanistic analysis of spatial reasoning in CLIP-style models while maintaining experimental control

Thorough attention decomposition analysis (Eq. 1-2) with clear visualization of horizontal gradients in positional-token cross-terms, backed by definitive ablations (Fig. 5e) showing necessity of these components
Surprising empirical finding that label diversity substantially outweighs layout diversity for generalization to unseen object pairs, challenging intuitive assumptions
Comprehensive evaluation across three well-defined generalization types with proper train-test separation, plus extensive ablations across architectural variants and positional encodings

Novel theoretical analysis extending findings to RoPE, identifying two distinct generalization mechanisms (bias-induced gradient and learned subspace alignment) with supporting evidence from PCA and singular value analysis
Excellent presentation quality with clear figures, comprehensive appendices, and transparent discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Extreme problem simplification (1D images, left-right relations only, artificial single-token text) creates substantial gap to realistic VLMs; unclear how findings transfer to 2D natural images and compositional language, with no concrete experimental pathway provided

Shallow models (1-4 Transformer blocks, 4 heads) studied; Appendix L acknowledges 2-layer analysis is incomplete, leaving uncertainty about mechanisms' scaling properties to realistic depths (e.g., ViT-B with 12 layers)

Modest unseen-pair generalization (~90-95% best case with high label diversity) and degraded performance with bilateral captions (Fig. 8) suggest mechanisms may be fragile or task-specific; unclear if robustness translates to natural settings

Text encoder analysis incomplete: Section 6 is brief, authors explicitly note 'complexity in interpreting 2-layer Transformer model' (p.8) remains unresolved, and alignment via learned rotation (Fig. 7) lacks principled explanation

RoPE mechanism verification is indirect (PCA/SVD analysis) rather than direct intervention; lacks empirical confirmation by explicitly manipulating model components (e.g., enforcing low-rank W_K) during training
Limited practical implications for improving real VLMs; no discussion of whether encouraging positional embeddings during training improves spatial reasoning, or guidance on architectural changes

Incomplete coverage of related work on positional encodings and spatial reasoning; no comparison with sinusoidal or other alternatives; connection to grokking phenomenon (Appendix B) mentioned but underdeveloped
Single-head vision transformer consistently fails (Appendix K); requirement for multi-head attention claimed but not mechanistically explained, limiting understanding of what properties are essential

strengths: Rigorous experimental design with well-controlled 1D synthetic testbed enabling systematic study of factors affecting spatial understanding

Thorough mechanistic analysis: attention logit decomposition (Eq. 1-2) clearly identifies that position-token embedding cross-terms (EP term) are essential for left-right discrimination, supported by convincing ablations
Comprehensive experiments spanning generalization dynamics, multi-head analysis, RoPE mechanisms, and detailed appendices—demonstrates scientific rigor
Theoretical contribution (Appendix I) providing formal justification for why position-dependent attention gradients are necessary for OOD generalization, extended to RoPE
Honest discussion of limitations acknowledging fundamental gaps between toy setting and real VLMs
weaknesses: Severe relevance gap: The 1D toy setting (single-pixel objects, length-10 images, only left/right relations) is far removed from real VLMs on natural 2D images. Critically, the paper does NOT demonstrate these mechanisms actually emerge in realistic models—this is left entirely to future work, fundamentally undermining the contribution

Unclear impact on stated problem: Paper motivates work by citing spatial reasoning failures in real VLMs (ARO, CLEVR, Winoground) but never validates that identified mechanisms operate in or explain these failures. Gap between '1D left-right learning' and 'real VLM spatial failures' is never bridged

Limited novelty: Core finding that 'label diversity matters more than layout diversity' is expected from generalization theory. Insight that positional embeddings enable spatial discrimination via attention gradients is reasonable but not surprising. Application of standard interpretability techniques to a constrained problem

Scaling concerns unresolved: Section 7 shows mechanistic analysis becomes intractable with 2-layer text encoder ('remains unclear due to complexity'). Appendix L acknowledges 2-layer vision encoders have intractable 'complex gradient patterns.' This suggests approach fails to scale to realistic models

Key findings relegated to appendices: Multi-head requirement (Appendix K) unexplored in main text despite being necessary for generalization. RoPE analysis interesting but mechanistic understanding is post-hoc. 2-layer dynamics deferred to future work

Simplified architecture undermines realism: Removal of LayerNorm/MLP for mechanistic analysis is justified but these components fundamentally affect spatial information processing in real Transformers. No analysis of whether these simplifications change what mechanisms emerge

Missing validation experiments: No demonstration on 2D synthetic data, no connection to real model failures, no test of whether understanding 1D mechanism predicts real VLM behavior. Severely limits ability to assess relevance
Modest experimental rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed reporting of results. How consistent are findings across random initializations?

strengths: Rigorous experimental design with a well-motivated 1D toy testbed that enables clean mechanistic analysis of spatial understanding
Thorough and novel mechanistic analysis identifying positional-token embedding interactions as critical for left-right symmetry breaking
Well-executed interpretability work including attention decomposition, ablations, and comparison of generalizing vs. non-generalizing models
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and honest discussion of limitations
Theoretical grounding (Appendix I) explaining why position-dependent gradients are necessary for OOD generalization, with extensions to modern positional encodings like RoPE
Strong finding that label diversity substantially outweighs layout diversity for generalization, suggesting interesting principles about semantic vs. positional variation
weaknesses: Severely limited scope—1D setting with only left-right relations and binary object pairs is far removed from realistic 2D spatial reasoning where the phenomenon actually matters
No empirical evidence that discovered mechanisms transfer to 2D images or more complex spatial relations, limiting practical applicability and generalizability
Key empirical finding (label >> layout diversity) lacks mechanistic explanation—why does semantic variety matter so much more than positional variety?
Architectural simplifications for mechanistic analysis (removing LayerNorm, MLP, using 1-layer models) reduce relevance to real models; 2-layer analysis acknowledged as incomplete
Theoretical analysis explains why position-dependent gradients are necessary but not why training discovers them—what loss signals drive this solution?
Limited practical implications for improving real VLMs on spatial reasoning tasks; paper contributes to understanding but not to system improvements
Important failure modes under-explored: why do 1-layer models fail with both left/right representations? Why is multi-head attention apparently necessary?
Some experimental gaps: the three generalization phases (Appendix C) are interesting but under-explored; connection to 'grokking' mentioned but not analyzed

strengths: Well-designed controlled 1D image-text testbed effectively isolates left-right spatial understanding mechanisms in a reproducible manner
Rigorous mechanistic analysis through attention logit decomposition (Eq. 1) systematically identifies contributions from token, positional, and bias components
Comprehensive ablation studies with multiple variants (weight decay, term removal, RoPE comparison, 2D/3D extensions) strengthen empirical findings
Clear mathematical framework for analyzing out-of-distribution generalization with explicit conditions (Eq. 14, 23) and validation (Figs. 19c-e)
Thorough documentation with 14 pages of appendices, clear hyperparameter specification, and reasonable reproducibility within controlled setting
Well-written paper with clear motivation, logical organization, and informative visualizations of attention patterns
weaknesses: Critical domain gap: 1D pixel-based synthetic setting is far removed from natural images; 2D extension (Appendix K) shows degraded performance with limited analysis, undermining claims about practical relevance

Oversimplified text representation using literal spatial descriptions (e.g., 'X is on the left of Y') rather than natural language; unclear how findings transfer to real VLM training with diverse linguistic descriptions

Limited evidence that discovered mechanisms generalize beyond synthetic data with learnable positional embeddings; RoPE-only variant (Fig. 18) shows substantially weaker results, suggesting findings are architecture-specific

Theoretical analysis of generalization mechanisms (especially Mechanism 2 on learned subspace alignment) relies on strong assumptions validated only indirectly through PCA analysis; causal claims lack definitive proof
Narrow scope limited to left-right relations in CLIP-style models; unclear whether mechanisms extend to other spatial relations, architectures, or VLM training paradigms
Unclear practical impact: no demonstration that mechanistic insights can improve spatial reasoning in real-world VLMs or downstream tasks; primarily of interest to interpretability specialists
No code release despite use of public codebases; integration details for 1D setting with standard frameworks incompletely specified

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: The paper identifies a concrete failure mode of CLIP-style models in distinguishing left-right spatial relations, with potential relevance to broader spatial reasoning limitations.
Elegant experimental design: The 1D synthetic image-text testbed enables precise control and interpretability, allowing clean mechanistic analysis of the identified phenomenon.

Comprehensive mechanistic analysis: Multiple layers of investigation including attention pattern visualization, logit component decomposition (EE, EP, PE, PP), and theoretical analysis of positional embeddings provide thorough mechanistic insight.

Extensive empirical investigation: Appendices cover numerous extensions (weight decay, generalization dynamics, RoPE analysis, 2D/3D extensions, autoregressive models), demonstrating genuine effort to understand the phenomenon broadly.
Clear presentation of mechanistic findings: Figures effectively communicate attention patterns and their role in symmetry breaking within the scope of the simplified setting.
weaknesses: Limited practical relevance: The core analysis uses synthetic 1D images with templated captions. The paper fails to demonstrate that real CLIP models exhibit this failure mode on actual spatial reasoning benchmarks (NLVR2, Winoground, ARO, etc.), leaving the practical significance unclear.

Gap between toy problem and real vision-language understanding: The 1D setting is far removed from realistic scenarios involving complex visual scenes, diverse caption phrasings, compositional reasoning, and ambiguous spatial references. Generalization claims are not adequately justified.

No proposed solutions or actionable insights: While the paper analyzes the problem extensively, it offers no practical solutions for practitioners. The observation that using both textual representations helps is incremental and relegated to appendices.

Post-hoc theoretical justification: The mathematical analysis in Appendix J explains empirical observations after the fact but doesn't provide fundamental insights into why the mechanism exists or why positional embeddings cause left-right bias specifically in this setting while working fine for standard vision-language tasks.

Weak generalization evidence: Extensions show poor transfer (e.g., 3-object generalization in Appendix N drops to ~15%), and failure modes in simpler settings (1-layer models in Appendix L) are inadequately explained, suggesting findings may not generalize beyond this specific architecture and training regime.

No evaluation on real benchmarks or real models: The paper lacks empirical validation that the identified mechanism explains real-world failures in deployed vision-language models or that findings apply to real visual scenes and natural language descriptions.

Incomplete analysis of design choices: The paper doesn't explain why other positional encoding schemes avoid this problem, why autoregressive models show dramatically better performance (94% vs. <60%), or whether the mechanism is specific to contrastive learning.

Statistical rigor concerns: Generalization curves lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It's unclear whether observed differences in learning curves are statistically meaningful or result from noise.

strengths: Novel mechanistic approach to understanding spatial reasoning in VLMs using controlled synthetic 1D image-text testbed, enabling precise analysis without confounding factors

Rigorous and thorough mechanistic analysis decomposing attention logits into interpretable components (token-dependent and position-dependent), clearly identifying how positional embeddings create left-right attention gradients

Comprehensive experimental work with extensive ablations and extensions (2D images, 3-object scenes, autoregressive VLMs, architecture variations, weight decay effects, LayerNorm analysis) demonstrating breadth of investigation
Strong empirical results showing ~98% unseen-pair generalization accuracy and the non-obvious finding that label diversity (not just layout diversity) is crucial for generalization
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-designed visualizations (particularly Figures 3-5), and logical progression from controlled experiments to realistic extensions
Strong reproducibility practices including detailed computational specifications, hyperparameters, public code repositories, and complete dataset descriptions enabling replication
weaknesses: Limited real-world relevance: synthetic 1D setting is far removed from practical vision-language tasks; 2D experiments use only 4×4 images and 3-object extension shows substantial performance degradation (~83% vs 98%+), with no evaluation on established spatial reasoning benchmarks

Narrow scope: investigation restricted to left-right relations only with generalization to other spatial relations (above/below, inside/outside) unexplored; focus on CLIP-style contrastive training with limited exploration of other VLM architectures

Theoretical justification could be stronger: while mechanistic analysis is thorough, lacks rigorous explanation of why positional embeddings should create left-right gradients; theoretical analysis in Appendix J limited to 1-layer models

Moderate practical impact: does not propose concrete methods to improve spatial reasoning based on findings; claim that label diversity drives generalization, while valuable, aligns with existing literature; implications for practitioners remain unclear

Incomplete analysis of text encoder: focus heavily skewed toward vision encoder attention with minimal investigation of text encoder's role and underdeveloped analysis of vision-text encoder alignment (Section 6.2)

Generalization limitations: all generalization types remain within synthetic domain; single-object positional generalization reaches saturation quickly (not a bottleneck); failure modes inadequately analyzed, particularly the 3-object extension performance drop

Missing comparisons: no direct comparison with alternative mechanistic theories of spatial reasoning in VLMs; limited connection to recent work on compositional reasoning and other interpretability studies
